idiom_name: structural implementor interface plus an injected field
implementation_notes: Interfaces are structural - types relate by their members, not by declaration - so the implementor contract needs no implements clause and an object literal, a third-party class or a function-shaped object all satisfy it; that structural contract plus an injected field is TypeScript's replacement for the nominal abstract-base structure. The abstraction is normally an abstract class with a protected readonly renderer, or a plain class with a constructor parameter property, and implements is documentation plus a check rather than the mechanism. The nominal hierarchy is still worth writing when you want shared forwarding code or a branded (private/protected) member that stops unrelated types from matching structurally by accident. Because types are erased at compile time the contract does not exist at runtime, so keep validation of untrusted implementors at the boundary.
pitfalls: Types are erased: nothing at runtime enforces the implementor contract, so an untyped caller can pass an object missing a primitive and the failure surfaces only at the call - validate at I/O boundaries.
Structural typing lets an unrelated class that happens to have a compatible method satisfy the implementor interface; add a private/protected branded member when the distinction matters.

abstract does not exist at runtime, so instanceof sees only concrete classes and abstract members can be reached through casts - TypeScript does not enforce the abstraction contract in JavaScript code paths.
